keyTerms.definition: Summing away hidden causes to score the observable marginal.
The tractable lower bound on the marginal log-likelihood.
A low-variance gradient through a sampler; a lesson objective.
One encoder for all points; a lesson objective.

recall.question: What does this lesson cover?
recall.answer: Models with hidden causes: latent marginalization, posterior, Bayes rule, Jensen inequality, the ELBO identity, the variational gap, KL direction, reparameterized gradients, Monte Carlo variance, amortization, expressive variational families, and degeneracy.

recall.question: What will the learner be able to do after this lesson?
recall.answer: Marginalize a discrete latent by hand, invert a likelihood with Bayes, derive the ELBO from Jensen, name the gap as a KL, predict mode-seeking versus mode-covering from the KL direction, and implement reparameterized gradients.

keyTerms.definition: z in {A, B}: the latent cause of the observed ball.
P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.4: the belief before the draw.

recall.question: State the four parameters of the toy.
recall.answer: Bag A: 80 percent red, 20 percent green. Bag B: 30 percent red, 70 percent green. Prior: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.4.

recall.question: What is observed?
recall.answer: One draw, and the ball is red: x = R.

keyTerms.definition: A hidden variable the model sums away; here the bag z in {A, B}.
p(x) = sum_z p(x,z): the law the data can see.
p(x) = sum_z p(x|z) p(z): each term is one hidden path.

recall.question: Compute P(R) for the two-bag toy.
Why can training only ever score the marginal?
recall.answer: The data show x, not z. The joint holds everything, but only the marginal is observable.

keyTerms.definition: p(z|x): the belief about the hidden cause after seeing the data.
The belief before the observation: (0.6, 0.4) here.

recall.question: Compute P(A|R) on the toy.
What question does the posterior answer?
recall.answer: What explains this observation, not what happens next.

keyTerms.definition: p(z|x) = p(x|z) p(z) / p(x): the machine from likelihoods to posteriors.
p(x): the denominator; it normalizes and scores the model itself.

recall.question: State Bayes rule and name each part.
recall.answer: p(z|x) = p(x|z) p(z) / p(x). The numerator is the joint; the denominator is the marginal from C01.

recall.question: What breaks Bayes?
recall.answer: An observation outside the model support: p(x) = 0 breaks the ratio.

keyTerms.definition: For convex phi, E[phi(X)] >= phi(E[X]); the direction flips for concave.
Log is concave, so E[log X] <= log E[X]: the engine of variational inference.

recall.question: State Jensen for concave log with the toy numbers.
Why is Jensen the engine of variational inference?
recall.answer: The log sits outside the marginalization sum; Jensen moves a tractable expectation inside.

keyTerms.definition: E_q[log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z)||p(z)): reconstruction minus regularization; a lower bound on log p(x).
log p(x) = ELBO + KL(q(z)||p(z|x)).

recall.question: Compute the ELBO decomposition on the toy.
recall.answer: Reconstruction -0.5174, KL(q||prior) 0.0216, ELBO = -0.5390.

recall.question: What are the two terms of the ELBO and their jobs?
recall.answer: E_q[log p(x|z)] rewards q for putting mass where data are likely; KL(q||p(z)) pulls q toward the prior.

keyTerms.definition: KL(q(z)||p(z|x)): the exact distance between the ELBO and log p(x).
ELBO equals log p(x) when q is the posterior.

recall.question: What is the gap for q = (0.7,0.3), q = posterior, q = prior?
recall.answer: 0.0282, 0, 0.1047 nats. The prior is the worst q of the three.

recall.question: Why does minimizing the gap equal maximizing the ELBO?
recall.answer: log p(x) = ELBO + gap, and log p(x) is constant in q.

keyTerms.definition: E_p[log p/q]: must cover every mode; mean-seeking, zero-avoiding.
E_q[log q/p]: must sit where p is; mode-seeking.

recall.question: Which fit wins under forward KL on the two-mode toy?
recall.answer: The cover q = N(0, 2.2^2): 0.632 versus 8.311 nats for the seek fit.

recall.question: What decides which law may have zeros?
recall.answer: The direction of the expectation. E_p punishes q zeros; E_q punishes p zeros under q mass.

keyTerms.definition: Separate randomness from parameters: gradients flow through g by the chain rule.
The naive gradient estimator: unbiased but too noisy for minibatches.

recall.question: Compare the two gradient estimators on the toy.
recall.answer: Reparam: mean 1.9781, std 0.1171. Score-function: mean 1.9165, std 0.2546. Both unbiased; one is usable in a minibatch.

recall.question: Which latents does reparameterization exclude?
recall.answer: Discrete latents do not qualify; only location-scale families and implicit-gradient cases do.

keyTerms.definition: O(1/sqrt(K)) regardless of dimension.
Shrinks like 1/sqrt(K): quadrupling K halves the noise.

recall.question: How many samples reach std 0.05 on the toy?
recall.answer: About K = 6400 by the 1/sqrt law: 0.1001 x sqrt(1600/6400) = 0.0501.

recall.question: What shrinks the constant versus the rate?
recall.answer: Reparameterization shrinks the constant. More samples shrink the rate term.

keyTerms.definition: One encoder network replaces per-point q_i optimization; inference becomes a forward pass.
The price: the encoder may not reach each point's best q.

recall.question: When does the encoder win on parameter count?
recall.answer: Per-point 4n versus 420 parameters: the encoder wins for n > 105.

recall.question: What is the test-time difference?
recall.answer: Per-point inference costs an optimization loop per point; amortized costs one forward pass.

keyTerms.definition: Diagonal Gaussians: factorize across dimensions; no correlation allowed.
The set q may belong to; a poor family leaves an irreducible gap.

recall.question: What is the irreducible gap on the correlated toy?
recall.answer: KL(N(0,Sigma)||N(0,I)) = 0.8304 nats. Full covariance drops it to 0.

recall.question: What does the upgrade cost?
recall.answer: d(d+1)/2 covariance parameters instead of d.

keyTerms.definition: Swapping latent labels with matching parameter moves leaves every marginal unchanged.
A symmetry direction in the likelihood that the data cannot see.

recall.question: Show the degeneracy on the toy.
recall.answer: Prior (0.4,0.6) with swapped likelihoods gives marginal 0.60, identical to the original. The data see the same number.

recall.question: What happens to the posterior over z under the swapped labeling?
recall.answer: It is the mirror image (0.2, 0.8): every observable matches, every label disagrees.

keyTerms.definition: B1 asks for the formula and P(R) on the toy.
L1 asks to derive it from Jensen and name the gap.
D1 asks to debug one that returns 0.0 on every step.
R1 attacks 'a higher ELBO always means a better generative model'.

recall.question: What does the L1 ladder cover?
recall.answer: Derive the ELBO from Jensen, name the gap, compute it on the toy, explain what happens when q equals the posterior, and design the grid experiment that checks ELBO plus gap is constant.

recall.question: What does T1 change?
recall.answer: A third bag with prior 0.1, the old priors scaled to 0.9, and P(R|C) = 0.5. Recompute the marginal, the posterior, and the ELBO at the old q padded with 0, and find what breaks in the q family.

recall.answer: Marginalization audit, posterior grid, ELBO identity check, reparam versus score-function shootout, amortization crossover, mean-field gap.
